speaker: alice
text: First up, one of the most heartwarming conservation stories we've heard in ages. <cite index='12-1,12-2'>Scientists from UNSW Sydney have confirmed that platypus population in Royal National Park has grown to 20 known individuals</cite>. <cite index='12-18,12-19'>Before 2023, platypuses were absent from the park for more than 50 years, and now visitors are reporting platypus sightings along the Hacking River</cite>.

speaker: charlie
text: That's absolutely bonkers in the best way. <cite index='13-20'>This is the first successful platypus translocation in New South Wales</cite>, and they've just added four more little fellas called Absinthe, Duckie, Hydra and Dawn. <cite index='13-18,13-19'>The scientists have found a new subadult hatched in the park, showing the population is breeding and has multiple age classes</cite>.

speaker: alice
text: The really beautiful bit is what researcher Gilad Bino said about <cite index='13-17'>that public connection, people seeing platypuses back where they belong, being one of the most rewarding outcomes</cite>. On the tech front, scientists have created <cite index='3-6,3-7'>special algae that can grab microscopic plastic pollution out of water almost like a magnet using limonene, an orange-scented oil</cite>.
